I've written the notes below, but there are gaps. My tool limit ran out partway through, so I couldn't find anything usable from the Lutheran or Wesley's Notes pages, from catholic.com, or on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this psalm. For some sources (Augustine, Calvin, Spurgeon, Sam Storms, Desiring God, the NET Bible, bible.org) I only saw part of the page in search results, not the full text.

# Psalm 63: Research Notes

## Title / setting
- **Guzik:** Most commentators place the psalm either in David's years hiding from Saul or in his flight from Absalom. Guzik prefers the Saul years but isn't certain. He passes on Spurgeon's note that, according to Chrysostom, the early church sang this psalm every day. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-63/
- **Gill:** He gives both settings (Saul or Absalom). He also reads the psalm as pointing to Christ hungry in the wilderness, to the church "in the wilderness" (Rev 12), and to all believers in dry seasons. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/63.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** It assumes the Absalom flight and links details to 2 Samuel 15–17. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/63.htm
- **Ellicott (a critical view):** He rejects the title. He thinks it came from misreading verse 1, which he takes as a figure of speech rather than a real desert. In his view it is better read as an exile longing for the temple, perhaps just before Jerusalem fell. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/63.htm
- **Augustine (Catholic/patristic):** His Latin title says "desert of Idumea." He takes Idumea to mean this world and this hard present life. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801063.htm
- **Orthodox use:** In Orthodox numbering this is Psalm 62. It is one of the Six Psalms read at the start of Matins, the church's morning service (alongside Pss 3, 37, 62, 87, 102, 142 in that numbering). https://www.oca.org/files/PDF/Music/Chat/2007/04.23.07.matins.pdf ; https://www.oca.org/files/PDF/Music/Rubrics/Horologion/office-daily-matins.pdf

## v. 1
- **"You are my God" is not empty repetition.** David declares that the God of all is his own God. Guzik cites Kidner: this personal bond is the heart of the covenant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-63/
- **Gill:** "My God" by grace and covenant, not merely by being born an Israelite. The Aramaic paraphrase (Targum) reads "Thou art my strength." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/63.htm
- **Pulpit:** The Hebrew *Eli* can mean "my strong God." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/63.htm
- **"Earnestly / early":** The verb is related to the Hebrew word for dawn.
  - Ellicott: the Greek and Latin Bibles read "to thee I wake early," meaning his first waking thoughts turn to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/63.htm
  - Gill: either "I will seek thee at morning" or "diligently," like a merchant hunting for pearls. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/63.htm
  - Spurgeon: the word means both early in the morning and eagerly, at once. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps063.cfm
- **Augustine:** "I watch" means the soul must not sleep, and the soul's sleep is forgetting God. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801063.htm
- **"Body yearns":** The Hebrew verb appears only here and may mean "pine" or "faint."
  - Ellicott and Pulpit: soul and flesh together mean the whole person, body and soul. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/63.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/63.htm
  - Poole, cited by Guzik: the longing is so strong the body feels it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-63/
- **"Dry and weary land":**
  - Gill: the Judean desert, where David was cut off from public worship. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/63.htm
  - Ellicott suggests reading "*as* a dry land": the parched land is a picture of the soul. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/63.htm
  - Spurgeon (via Guzik): there was a desert around him but none in his heart. Don't wait to feel better before you pray. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-63/

## v. 2
- **Guzik:** David wasn't at the tabernacle when he wrote this. He knew God's sanctuary could also be entered by faith from anywhere. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-63/
- **Gill:**
  - Jewish interpreters take "power and glory" to mean the ark.
  - Gill prefers Christ, "the power of God" and the brightness of his glory, seen in the word and ordinances.
  - Past experiences of worship make David hungry for more. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/63.htm
- **Ellicott:** Translate it "So in the sanctuary have I had vision of thee." The verb is the one usually used for prophetic vision, so David had a spiritual sight of God beyond the outward symbols. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/63.htm
- **Pulpit:** David longs to see God worshipped in the sanctuary again, as he had before. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/63.htm
- **bible.org (Utley):** The snippet I saw gives a second option, that the verse describes a vision of God himself as in Isaiah 6 or Ezekiel 1. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-63

## v. 3: where interpreters differ
- **Guzik:** The *hesed* (loyal, covenant love) of God was worth more to David than his own life. Brooks, quoted via Spurgeon: no one ever grew weary of God's favour. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-63/
- **Gill:** Life without God's love is a kind of death. God's love outlasts life, and martyrs prove it by giving up their lives. The Targum applies the verse to the world to come. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/63.htm
- **Ellicott:** *Hesed* here means covenant favour, and knowing it is better than the joy of being alive. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/63.htm
- **Pulpit:** The psalmist's resignation and praise, where he might have complained, are a pattern for the church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/63.htm
- **Augustine vs. Calvin on the plural "lives":**
  - Augustine (Catholic/patristic): The Hebrew "lives" points to the many lives people choose for themselves, such as business, farming or soldiering. God's one promised life is better, and it is given by mercy, not merit. God's mercy justifies the sinner, and even our praise is his gift. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801063.htm
  - Calvin (Reformed): He rejects Augustine's reading as clever but groundless, because the Hebrew plural simply means "life." He also calls the plain "God's favour beats every possession" reading thin. For him the contrast is between the secure prosperity people rest in and God's mercy, which holds up those who are about to sink. We should trust that mercy "in the midst of death" more than anything that looks like life. https://www.ccel.org/study/Psalm_63:1-4
- **Clarke (Methodist):** This is the language of every regenerate soul, though few really prefer God's approval to life. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/63-3.html
- **Coffman (Restoration Movement):** Thousands of martyrs confirm the verse. Same URL.
- **Note on the Hebrew (NET Bible):** "Because" can be taken as giving the reason for the praise, or as emphatic ("Indeed, your loyal love is better…"). NET also adds the word "experiencing" to its translation. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=ps+63%3A3-4

## v. 4: where traditions differ on lifted hands
- **Guzik:** Raised hands were the usual Hebrew posture for prayer and especially fitted praise. They show expectation of receiving from God and surrender to him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-63/
- **Gill:** Some Jewish interpreters (Kimchi) take it as lifting hands against enemies. Gill instead reads it as hands raised to God in blessing or prayer. The Targum says "in the name of thy Word," which Gill takes as praying in the Messiah's name. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/63.htm
- **Pulpit:** The purpose of human life, and our main work in eternity, is praising God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/63.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed):** The raised hands point to prayer and vows. Gratitude for past goodness should make us pray more confidently for the future. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/63-4.html
- **Sam Storms (charismatic):** He lifts his hands because Psalm 63:4 and many other texts give explicit biblical precedent. In his view prayer and worship can't be strictly separated, and raised hands confess utter dependence on God. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/i-will-lift-up-my-hands--psalm-63:4- ; https://www.samstorms.org/enjoying-god-blog/post/10-things-you-should-know-about-the-lifting-of-hands-in-worship
- **John Piper (Baptist):** He cites Psalm 63:4 but says his church never created an atmosphere where people were expected to raise hands "if you're spiritual." In his view the point of 1 Timothy 2:8 is that the hands be *holy*. https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/should-we-raise-our-hands-in-worship ; https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/should-men-still-pray-with-lifted-hands
- **Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel):** He uses the verse to criticise stiff, formal worship and to urge believers to raise their hands. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/63-4.html

## v. 5
- **Guzik:** The deep satisfaction of seeking God with full surrender. Spurgeon: God's love is like the richest food. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-63/
- **Gill:** The "fatness of thy house" (Ps 36:8). It must be meant spiritually, since the Law forbade eating fat. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/63.htm
- **Pulpit vs. Ellicott on the sacrificial feasts:**
  - Pulpit: the psalmist remembers the sacrificial feasts, but only as a shadow of the deeper joy of spiritual worship and praise. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/63.htm
  - Ellicott: the banquet image need not be tied to the sacrificial feasts at all. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/63.htm
- **Calvin:** David was sure of abundant blessing even while poor in the wilderness. He isn't picturing the self-indulgence of the ungodly. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/63-5.html
- **Barnes:** Serving God is compared to the pleasure of food when one is hungry (compare Isa 25:6). Same URL.
- **Spurgeon (quoted in Treasury):** God satisfies his people when he feeds them with new-covenant promises. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps063.cfm

## v. 6
- **Night watches:**
  - Ellicott: the Hebrew text says "beds." The Jewish night had three watches (beginning, middle, morning). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/63.htm
  - Gill: the plural "beds" fits David's many hiding places (so Kimchi). Three Jewish watches against four Roman ones. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/63.htm
- **Pulpit:** It suggests the psalm was composed during a sleepless night and sung at dawn (2 Sam 16:14). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/63.htm
- **Kidner and Horne (via Guzik):** The phrase stresses how slowly the hours pass. The stillness of night suits remembering God's mercies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-63/

## v. 7
- **Guzik:** The psalm gives thanks for past help rather than crying for help. On "wings" he weighs protection (a mother bird) against presence (the cherubim's wings over the ark) and prefers presence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-63/
- **Gill:** He leans to protection, like chicks under a hen. The Targum reads "shadow of thy Shechinah" (God's presence), meaning the cherubim over the mercy seat. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/63.htm
- **Pulpit:** Past rescues give confidence for the future. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/63.htm

## v. 8
- **"Clings":** The Hebrew is literally "cleaves after you," the same verb as Genesis 2:24 (a man "cleaves" to his wife).
  - Ellicott and Gill: Gill draws out union with Christ, like head and members or vine and branches. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/63.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/63.htm
  - Guzik, citing Chandler: the word means "glue together." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-63/
- **Pulpit:** The action goes both ways. The soul presses close while God's right hand holds it, as in an embrace. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/63.htm

## v. 9
- **"Depths of the earth":**
  - Ellicott: the underworld of the dead. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/63.htm
  - Gill: hell, not just the grave. He notes Kimchi reads it as a wish ("let them go") and sees a possible echo of Korah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/63.htm
- **Praying against enemies:** Pulpit admits, citing Cheyne, that the psalmist sees no conflict between devotion and condemning his foes. It explains that he sees them as God's and Israel's enemies, and asks only that they be removed, not tormented. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/63.htm
- **Guzik:** Communion with God didn't remove David's dangers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-63/

## v. 10
- **"Fall to the power of the sword":** Ellicott and Gill note the Hebrew literally means "pour him out by the hands of the sword." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/63.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/63.htm
- **Who fell:**
  - Gill: Saul and his sons (1 Sam 31), and in a further sense antichrist (Rev 13, 19). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/63.htm
  - Pulpit: Absalom's army (2 Sam 18:6–8). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/63.htm
- **"Foxes" should be "jackals"** (Ellicott, Pulpit). Kidner, via Guzik, calls them the last scavengers of a kill and says God's love is "strong with justice." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-63/

## v. 11
- **Who is "the king"?**
  - Guzik: David, not yet on the throne, speaking in faith from his anointing (1 Sam 16). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-63/
  - Pulpit: the author speaking of himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/63.htm
  - Gill: David, or "rather" Christ the King Messiah. He notes a Jewish view (R. Obadiah) that it means Saul. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/63.htm
  - Ellicott: a king of Judah near the exile. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/63.htm
- **"Swear by Him":**
  - Ellicott: this could mean swearing loyalty to the king, but more naturally it means swearing by the LORD (Deut 6:13), that is, being loyal to him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/63.htm
  - Gill: it stands for all true worship. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/63.htm
  - Guzik: trusting God, as opposed to lying. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-63/
- **"Liars":**
  - Pulpit: the slanders against David in 2 Samuel 15–16. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/63.htm
  - Gill: Saul's courtiers, and finally antichrist's followers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/63.htm
